glossary.hint: Tap any label for what it means.
glossary.default: troid's default — change it to yours.
glossary.firm.what: The prop firm whose rules troid applies.
glossary.firm.ex: choose {firm} and every limit below is {firm}'s.
glossary.challenge.ex: {firm} "{product}" is a single phase with a {target}% target (read {date}).
glossary.quota.what: The size of the account you bought. Every percentage rule is measured from it.
glossary.quota.also: account size, initial balance, starting balance, funded amount
glossary.equity.what: What the account is worth right now, including open trades.
glossary.equity.also: account equity, current equity, floating balance, NAV
glossary.equity.ex: balance 101,200 with an open trade down 300 → equity 100,900. Firms count that open loss.
glossary.daystart.what: Your balance when the firm's trading day began. Daily limits are measured from here.
glossary.daystart.ex: you ended the last trading day at 100,900 with nothing open → day start 100,900. (The reset time is on each firm's column in troid's compare.)
glossary.hirollover.what: The higher of your balance and your equity when the firm's trading day rolled over. Where a firm measures the daily limit from it, the daily floor sits a fixed amount below it.
glossary.hirollover.also: daily high, max(balance, equity) at the reset
glossary.hirollover.ex: balance 100,900 and equity 101,300 at the reset → 101,300.
glossary.hirollover.formula: daily floor = high at rollover − quota × daily %
glossary.hwm.what: The highest your account has reached. On trailing-drawdown products the floor follows it up.
glossary.hwm.ex: the account reached 104,000, then fell back to 102,500 → the high-water mark is still 104,000.
glossary.hwm.formula: trailing floor = high-water mark − quota × max %
glossary.side.what: Long: you buy, and profit if price rises. Short: you sell, and profit if it falls.
glossary.side.note: Not the same as calls and puts. Those are options: you pay a premium for the right to buy (call) or sell (put) later, and the most you can lose is the premium. troid's desk sizes positions where the loss grows with every move against you until the stop — it doesn't model options.
glossary.entry.chip: For crypto, tap the live price under the field to use it.
glossary.stop.what: The price where you'd close to cap the loss. Below entry for a long, above it for a short.
glossary.stop.ex: long at 77,872, stop at 74,814 → 3,058 below entry.
glossary.target_r.what: Your profit target as a multiple of your stop distance.
glossary.target_r.formula: target = entry ± target R × stop distance
glossary.risk_pct.what: How much of your account you'd lose if the stop is hit.
glossary.risk_pct.ex: 0.5 on equity of 100,000 → $500 at the stop.
glossary.cap_pct.what: troid's own safety rule, not a firm's: one trade may use at most this share of the room left before your nearest limit.
glossary.cap_pct.ex: $4,000 of room at 35 → no single trade risks more than $1,400. After losses the room shrinks, so each trade shrinks with it instead of breaching the floor.
glossary.leverage.what: How much position each dollar of margin controls. It changes margin and liquidation distance — not the loss at your stop.
glossary.leverage.ex: a $12,478 position at 5× ties up $2,496 of margin. At 2× it ties up $6,239 — same loss at the stop either way.
glossary.mode.what: Cross: your whole account backs every position. Isolated: each position has its own margin and can be liquidated on its own.
glossary.mode.also: cross margin / shared margin; isolated margin / position margin
glossary.mode.ex: under cross at 5× with a normal stop, the firm's loss floor is reached long before the exchange would liquidate — so the stop is the only thing in front of the floor.
glossary.asset.what: What you're trading. It sets the firm's hold limit and whether the firm lists it; the size troid computes is the same for every asset.
glossary.verdict.what: OK, REDUCE or BLOCK — whether your trade fits, was cut to fit, or can't be sized.
glossary.binding.what: Whichever limit is closer right now: the daily limit or the max-loss floor. The one that would stop you first.
glossary.binding.live: {daily} of room before the daily limit, {dd} before the max-loss floor: the {bind} is closer.
glossary.crossover.what: Crossover: the equity where the two limits swap which one binds, on products with a static floor and a daily limit fixed from the starting balance.
glossary.room.what: Dollars between your equity and the binding ceiling.
glossary.size.what: How much of the asset to buy or sell. Under it, the notional: the position's full value.
glossary.size.also: position size, quantity, units, lots; notional: position value, exposure
glossary.size.formula: size = risk ÷ (stop distance + round-trip fee per unit)
glossary.margin.what: What's set aside for the position while it's open. The notional is its full value.
glossary.risk.what: What you'd lose at the stop, fees included: your risk %, cut to troid's cap when it's above it.
glossary.risk.formula: risk = min(equity × risk %, room × budget cap %)
glossary.fees.what: The share of your risk the exchange takes. Tighter stops make it larger.
glossary.fees.pending: This product's fee isn't recorded yet, so fees aren't counted.
glossary.stopd.what: How far your stop is from entry, as a share of the entry price. Under it, the price your target R reaches.
glossary.budget.what: How much of the room left this one trade would use.
glossary.left.what: How many losses of this size before the binding limit trips.
glossary.breakers.what: Everything that can stop a losing trade, in the order it would happen as price moves against you.
glossary.daily.what: The most the firm lets you lose in one trading day. Cross it and the account fails.
glossary.daily.live: floor {floor} ({formula}), {room} below your equity: a {pct} move against this position.
glossary.floor.what: The lowest your equity may ever go. Touch it and the account fails. A static floor stays put; a trailing one follows your high-water mark up.
glossary.floor.also: max drawdown, maximum loss, overall loss limit
glossary.floor.live: floor {floor} ({formula}), {room} below your equity: a {pct} move against this position.
glossary.liq.what: Where the exchange closes the position for lack of margin. Under cross margin at sane sizes the firm's floor comes first.

index.does.p:
Computes both loss ceilings and reports the binding one. Sizes positions net of the
  firm's own fee. Checks trades against each firm's own rules as troid has read them: its hold limit, its margin
  concentration limit, its minimum trading days. Works across the challenge types on troid's compare and the assets
  troid has read in each firm's own documents; troid's compare shows each rule with its source.
index.doesnt.p: Publish trade signals. Place orders. Touch your credentials. Sell you a strategy.
index.doesnt.tools: TROID.md is troid's rules and arithmetic as one file — paste it into any assistant as a system prompt. The MCP server does the same for Claude Desktop or Cursor, with exact arithmetic.
index.doesnt.verify: Every figure here shows its tier and source; the arithmetic reproduces in verify_claims.py, which re-derives each published number from first principles and tags it by tier — derived, sourced, modelled, or measured. A measured number is never stated as fact.

dashboard.meta.title: troid's research — strategy review
dashboard.og.title: troid's research — strategy review
dashboard.og.description: The strategy review and the audit findings, each number with its tier. Nothing here is a signal.
dashboard.hero.eyebrow: troid's research · strategy review · tearsheet · methodology
dashboard.hero.meta: MEASURED on BTCUSDT 4h bars from api.binance.us, one feed · under the rules of Bitfunded's 1-Step, Expert level, $100,000 · figures as of 21 Sep 2026
dashboard.verdict.big: Five-tranche strength ladder + regime filter + desk cap — but do not buy a challenge. The walk-forward has been run, and it came back as noise.
dashboard.verdict.p1: Of everything tested it has the lowest drawdown (−$1,058 against −$7,295 for single entry), and across 72 rolling challenge starts none failed, none stalled and none passed: every one was still running at the end of the sample, median balance $100,409. It is +0.03R a trade on the sample it was chosen on, and +0.008R on the 504 BTC trades from 1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026 it never saw. That is a well-built vehicle with no engine in it.
dashboard.verdict.p2: Why not: a $999 challenge buys one noisy binary outcome. Five years of holdout just said the entry logic has no measurable edge. At the 14% pass rate in FPFX Tech's data (SOURCED · reported by Finance Magnates, published {published}, read {read}; Sources), passing once barely updates whether you have an edge — plenty of edgeless traders pass.
dashboard.xref.h2: What the research found, including where troid was wrong
dashboard.xref.f1.h3: 1. A 5-tranche ladder holds less, not more
dashboard.xref.f1.p1: At the same $500 risk, a 5-tranche strength ladder holds 34% less quantity than a single entry (0.109 BTC against 0.167 BTC on a 1.5-ATR stop). Because the stop stays anchored at the first tranche's structure, each later tranche sits further from the stop and therefore gets less size.
dashboard.xref.f1.p2: The ladder's benefit is conditionality, not size: losers fill 1.66 tranches, winners fill 4.26. You're small when wrong and large when right. If what you actually want is a bigger position, that comes from raising risk per trade, and the ruin math says don't.
dashboard.xref.f2.h3: 2. troid's income model assumed about three times the real trade frequency
dashboard.xref.f2.p1: troid's income model (income_math.py) assumed 30 trades a month. The strategy produces 10.1 a month (78 trades in 7.7 months), so each account earns about a third of what the model showed.
dashboard.xref.f2.p2: At 10.1 trades a month and 0.5% risk, $6,250 a month gross needs +1.24R per trade ($6,250 ÷ $500 ÷ 10.1), far above the +0.008R the strategy measured out of sample. Either the timeframe drops below 4h to trade more often, or the target needs more accounts.
dashboard.xref.f3.h3: 3. The published statistics are generated, never written by hand
dashboard.xref.f3.p1: The results table was once written by hand, and it drifted from the engine after every change. It is now generated by gen_results.py from the engine on the frozen sample, and verify_claims.py re-derives the published statistics from journal.csv and fails if either drifts. The table below is that output.
dashboard.xref.f4.h3: 4. The rollover trap needs two conditions at once
dashboard.xref.f4.p1: Holding a position through the daily reset is often described as broadly dangerous. Measured over 72 rolling challenge starts for each of the 10 configurations, no position carried across a reset broke the $4,000 daily limit. The closest took uncapped 4% risk and a policy that holds losing positions through the reset together: a $3,448 floating loss against the $4,000 line. With troid's desk sizing the worst was $431; with its holding policy, which closes a losing position before the reset, none was carried.
dashboard.xref.f5.h3: 5. The reversal trigger moved to the stop-out; still one regime
dashboard.xref.f5.p1:
Triggered on the third target, the reverse fired 5 times in 7.7 months, because only
    about 9% of trades reach it. Triggered on the stop-out, it fires 24 times in the 78-trade sample, which is a sample
    rather than an anecdote, but it is still one asset over one regime, and the holdout (1 January 2021 to 7 January
    2026) says the whole configuration is inside noise.
dashboard.xref.f6.p1: Everything is in troid's public repository, kunjancollective/troid, and troid's ledger runs daily from .github/workflows/shadow.yml: fresh bars, replay, journal, ledger, commit. Each journal row is committed when it is logged, with its logged_utc, so the repository's history shows when every trade was recorded.
dashboard.xref.f7.h3: 7. Two known defects in troid's tools, not yet fixed
dashboard.xref.f7.p1: In income_math.py, the option that keeps profits in the account reports no income by construction, because it counts only withdrawals, so it can't be compared with withdrawing. And risk.py reads --json only before its subcommand.
dashboard.variants.h2: Where each variant stands — corrected numbers
dashboard.variants.note:
Ladder direction, the side the tranches sit on with the same signals and stops, moves
  the results more than any other change in the table. Weakness at 5 tranches has the worst profit factor
  (0.14); strength at 5 with the reverse on the stop has the smallest drawdown (−$1,058).
dashboard.risk.h2: Risk model: the firm's rules, the same whatever the strategy
dashboard.risk.reset.n: noon in New York, 11:00 in winter
dashboard.risk.p: The budget cap is not conservatism: it is what makes the account survivable. At +0.35R, a genuinely excellent system, naive sizing at 1% blows the account 68% of the time within a year, and at 2% it's 100%. Under the cap, every one of those cells is 0%.
dashboard.change.li1: Walk-forward comes back >+0.10R out-of-sample with a stable parameter neighbourhood. This is the gate on everything else. Run 21 Sep 2026 on api.binance.us: the config was chosen on 2026; on the 504 BTC trades from 1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026 it never saw, +0.008R, 95% CI [−0.023R, +0.040R]. ETH, 498 trades: +0.008R. Not met (MEASURED: WALKFORWARD.md).
dashboard.change.li2: Frequency reaches about 30 trades a month, the rate the income model assumed, which on this structure means dropping below the 4h timeframe.
dashboard.change.li3: Reverse moves to TP2 or stop-out so the exhaustion thesis gets a real sample instead of 5 trades. Done: reverse-on-stop is the config, 24 reverse trades in the sample (RESULTS.md). It did not change the verdict.
dashboard.next.p: troid's own strategy has been tested on five years of data it never saw, and measures inside noise: no measurable edge. Next:
dashboard.next.li1: A second strategy, troid-shadow-2, built separately so the first stays as it was: momentum over months, position size set by volatility, and the same loss limits and firm rules.
dashboard.next.li2: Both strategies across at least 10 assets, not only BTC. A rule that works on BTC alone was fitted to BTC.
dashboard.next.li3: The same walk-forward test for both, reported side by side. If neither survives it, that is the finding, and troid says so.
dashboard.next.li4: Whether troid ever trades a challenge with its own strategy waits on that result.
dashboard.foot: The sample: 1,539 4h bars, 8 Jan – 21 Sep 2026, api.binance.us (backtest/data/btc_4h.csv), one asset, one regime. The holdout, 1 January 2021 to 7 January 2026 (backtest/WALKFORWARD.md), came back inside noise on BTC and ETH.
faq.meta.title: troid — what the numbers actually say
faq.og.title: troid — what the numbers actually say
faq.og.description: Pass rates, costs, why accounts fail and how sizing decides survival, each figure with its tier.
faq.hero.lede: Base rates, rule mechanics and troid's own conflicts — the things a landing page leaves out.
faq.pass.q: What percentage of people actually pass?
faq.pass.p1: Data from FPFX Tech, a company that sells software to prop firms, reported by Finance Magnates in September 2024, covers more than 300,000 accounts from 100,000 traders at 10 firms. 14% of those traders passed a challenge and reached a funded account. About 45% of them were then paid: 7% of all traders. The average payout was 4% of the account size.
faq.cost.q: What does it really cost to get funded?
faq.cost.p1: In the same data, an account spent an average of $800 on challenge purchases over its whole life, typically across three challenges.
faq.cost.p2: Put the numbers together: 93% of the traders in that data were never paid, so for them the fees were a loss. That is what the published figures say about those traders, not a forecast for anyone.
faq.fail.p1: One firm, OneFunded, has published its own figures: 93.7% of its failed evaluations ended on a loss limit — 78.7% on the daily loss limit, 15.0% on the overall maximum — and 6.3% on inactivity and other rules. Its breaches cluster in the opening session and near the profit target, when traders enlarge positions to reach it.
faq.fail.p2:
OneFunded's own reading of those figures: “The problem is not always the strategy. More often, it comes
down to risk management issues.”
faq.offer.q: Then what is troid actually offering?
faq.offer.p1:
A free, open risk tool and the research behind it. It sizes positions against both of
a firm's loss ceilings at once, net of fees, and tells you which one is actually
binding. It does not publish trade signals and it will never place a trade.
faq.offer.p2:
troid built it because the failure data points at sizing, not entries. Whether you use
troid's desk, someone else's tool, or a spreadsheet, the arithmetic is the part worth getting
right.
faq.sec.rules: Things worth knowing about the rules
faq.challenge.q: What is a prop challenge, really?
faq.challenge.p: A prop challenge is an evaluation you pay for. The account you trade is usually a demo account. Your orders do not reach a real market, and the balance is not money you own. If you pass, the firm may pay you a share of simulated profits, on its own terms. In general, the firm is not a broker and holds no client funds. The fee buys the evaluation. It is not a deposit. So, in most cases, no broker regulation, client-money rule or investor-compensation scheme protects the account. Apart from the general consumer-protection law where you live, your protections are the firm's contract and nothing else. Read the contract before you pay: who you are contracting with, which country's law applies, what ends an account, and when a payout can be refused. A few firms also offer a route through a real exchange account. Check which kind you are buying.
faq.daily.q: What is your daily loss limit really?
faq.daily.p1: On a $100,000 1-Step account it is a fixed $4,000 — 4% of the initial balance, not of the day's starting balance. The day's loss is measured from your balance at the reset, and it counts floating losses on open positions, not just closed ones.
faq.daily.p2: But it often is not the constraint that matters. The 6% maximum loss is static at $94,000. Below roughly $98,000 of equity, the distance to that static floor is smaller than your daily allowance, so the max loss becomes the real ceiling and the "4% daily" number is fiction.
faq.daily.p3:
On a fresh account that crossover is about $2,000 away — half of one day's loss limit. Size
against the smaller of the two, always.
faq.reset.q: When does your trading day reset?
faq.reset.p1: 00:00 UTC+8, which is 16:00 UTC — noon in New York in summer, 11:00 in winter — not midnight. For a trader in New York the reset lands mid-session, so a morning loss and an afternoon loss can fall on different trading days and draw on different daily budgets. The platform's settlement can delay the reset by up to ten minutes, to 16:10 UTC, so don't count on a fresh daily budget before then.
faq.reset.p2:
The trap: a floating loss that survives the reset counts in full against the new day,
because the previous day's profit does not carry over. A position comfortably inside the
limit a minute before the reset can breach a minute after it without price moving at all. Bitfunded documents this
themselves.
faq.risk.q: How much should you risk per trade?
faq.risk.p1:
The right number depends on your system, so troid is not going to give you one.
What it can show you is what the arithmetic does to the wrong one.
faq.risk.p2: troid simulated a trader with an edge of +0.35R per trade: 45% of trades won at 2:1. Risking 1% per trade with no cap on remaining budget, that trader blew the account 68% of the time within twelve months. At 2%, 100%: every simulated year. Capping each trade at a fraction of the remaining budget rather than a fixed slice of the balance took all of those to 0%.
faq.risk.p3:
A real edge is not enough on its own. Under a 4%/6% rule set, position sizing decides
whether you survive long enough to use it.
faq.risk.src: MODELLED: 20,000 simulated years of 30 trades a month, 45% won at 2:1, under a 4% daily limit fixed on the $100,000 start and a 6% static floor; the cap is 35% of the remaining budget a trade. True under these assumptions only. income_math.py
faq.fees.p1:
More than most people model. Bitfunded charges 0.04% of position size on entry and
again on exit, calculated on notional — which at 5× leverage is five times your margin.
faq.fees.p2: Because notional scales inversely with stop distance, tight stops are punished hardest. A stop 3.9% away costs about 2% of your risk budget in fees. A 0.3% scalp stop costs 21%. On a $500 risk that is $105 gone before price moves.
faq.money.p1: Two ways, and only one exists yet.
faq.money.p2: troid is an independent affiliate of the firms it compares. When someone buys a challenge through one of its links or codes, that firm pays troid a commission. It's paid on the purchase, not on your result — troid would be paid if you failed. Where a code is shown, it's cheaper through the affiliate link; where it isn't, it's the same price. That's worth knowing, and worth weighing everything on this site against. Which firms, and the criterion for choosing them, is stated on troid's compare and reviewed quarterly.
faq.money.p3:
The second way, later, is a paid tier for people who want more than troid's desk — the
MCP server, journal analysis, multi-account tracking. That revenue doesn't depend on
anyone buying a challenge, which is deliberate.
faq.trust.q: Why should you trust any of this?
faq.trust.p1:
Don't, on troid's say-so. Everything above is checkable: the pass-rate data is published,
Bitfunded's rules are in their own documentation, and troid's backtest code is open — you can
run it and get the same numbers, including the unflattering ones.
faq.trust.p2: troid's ledger publishes its own results every four hours, losses included. troid's own strategy tested out of sample at +0.008R over 504 trades (MEASURED: WALKFORWARD.md) — no measurable edge — and the page says so.
faq.keep.q: Does troid keep my conversation with ask troid?
faq.keep.p: Yes, for 30 days. Each conversation is kept under a random session ID, shown under the message box, and deleted automatically 30 days after its last message. troid keeps your messages, ask troid's replies, the tools it used with their inputs and results, the rule sources and read dates it cited, the page's language and the AI model used; never your IP address, your browser's user agent, your name or an account. It keeps them to answer disputes about what ask troid said, to correct errors, to check that ask troid keeps to its guardrails, and to learn which questions come up most so troid can improve its pages and answers: once a week it counts them by topic, never quoting a message. Only troid's operator can read the stored conversations. Each message is sent to Anthropic to generate the answer, under Anthropic's API terms. They are never sold and never used for marketing or to train an AI model. To delete a conversation sooner, use “delete this conversation” under the message box, or write to hello@troid.ai with the session ID. Section 10 of troid's terms has the detail.
faq.track.p: No. troid sets no cookies and runs no analytics. The moving price tape at the top of each page is TradingView's: your browser loads it from TradingView's servers, which see your IP address and the page it sits on. TradingView's privacy policy covers that connection. With your device set to reduce motion, the tape isn't loaded unless you press play; pausing it takes it off the page.
faq.fill.q: Can troid fill in the price?
faq.fill.p:
For crypto, yes — tap "use" under Entry. The price there is the asset's spot price from Binance.US, asked about
every 15 seconds and marked "delayed" once it is over a minute old. A symbol tapped on the tape at the top of the page
opens the desk with that asset selected. Not for gold, oil or stocks at this time; type the price from the tape. Their
prices there are TradingView's, inside its own frame, and troid can't read them. A stock no compared firm offers, like
NVDA, opens the desk but can't be sized, because there are no firm rules to size it against. troid never fills in a
stop: the stop, the size and the trade stay yours.
faq.worth.p1:
troid doesn't answer that for anyone; it prices what you bring. The arithmetic is the same for every
reader: a trader who cannot state an edge, an average win-to-loss ratio, and the losing streak their
sizing survives will find those out from a challenge ({fee} for {firm}'s {quota} {product}, read {date}) faster than from a
spreadsheet at no cost.
The base rates on this page are the rest of it.
faq.worth.p2: troid's compare has the affiliate links and codes, and the criterion for which firms are on it. They're how troid is funded, and they cost you nothing extra. Direct is the same price where no code is shown.
faq.disc.advice.p:
Everything on this site is general information and education. It is not financial,
investment, trading, tax, or legal advice, and it does not account for your circumstances,
objectives, or risk tolerance. troid and the people who run it are not licensed financial advisors, brokers, or
registered investment professionals. Consult a qualified professional before making
financial decisions.
faq.disc.affiliate.p: troid is an independent affiliate of the firms it compares. It earns a commission on challenge purchases made through its links or discount codes. It is not an employee, agent or representative of any firm, and no firm owns or operates this website or is responsible for its contents. The current firms, and the criterion for choosing them, are on troid's compare.
faq.disc.simulated.p: Prop challenges and funded accounts are generally simulated trading environments. {question} above says what that means for your protections. Read the firm's terms yourself.
faq.disc.hypo.p: The hypothetical-performance disclosure, in the regulator's own words, is in troid's terms, section 6, and beside every result on troid's ledger and troid's research. troid's published backtests cover BTC and ETH on one exchange feed; the out-of-sample test showed no measurable edge, and troid publishes that result rather than the in-sample one.
faq.disc.eval.p1:
Challenge fees are generally non-refundable if you fail. Breaching a firm rule can
void accrued profits, terminate the account, or trigger a payout penalty — not merely
end the evaluation. Firms change their terms, and troid's rule summaries can lag those
changes.
faq.disc.eval.p2: Nothing troid publishes is a substitute for reading the firm's own Terms of Use. Where the two disagree, the contract governs — troid has already found one case where a firm's own challenge page displays a figure that contradicts its Terms.
faq.disc.eval.p3:
Two rules deserve specific attention because they are commonly missed. Bitfunded's
Terms prohibit using third-party or marketed strategies to pass an evaluation, so buying
a strategy, bot, or signal service and running it on a challenge may place you in breach
regardless of how it performs. And traders are limited to one active account per
challenge level absent written consent, which caps multi-account plans well below what
most people assume.
faq.disc.eval.p4:
troid's tools compute arithmetic against rules as it understands them at the time of
writing. They cannot detect a rule it has not modelled, a term that changed after
publication, or a firm-specific interpretation. Verify anything material with the firm
directly — Bitfunded provides support tickets for rule clarification.
faq.disc.eval.p5:
Beyond the affiliate relationship above, troid is not affiliated with, employed by, endorsed by, or authorised to speak for any
prop firm.
faq.disc.risk.p:
Trading leveraged cryptocurrency carries substantial risk. Most participants in prop
firm evaluations do not receive a payout. Challenge fees are generally non-refundable.
Never risk money you cannot afford to lose.
faq.disc.software.p:
troid's tools are provided as-is, without warranty of any kind. They perform arithmetic on
numbers you supply. They do not place, modify, or close trades, and they never handle
account credentials. You are responsible for verifying any output before acting on it.
faq.disc.jurisdiction.p:
Availability and legality of prop firm services vary by country. It is your
responsibility to confirm you are eligible to participate where you live.

faq.daily.derived: troid's arithmetic on the $100,000 account: 4% × $100,000 = $4,000; the floor, $100,000 × (1 − 6%) = $94,000; the crossover, $100,000 × (1 − 6% + 4%) = $98,000, $2,000 below the start.
faq.fees.derived: troid's arithmetic: a trade sized so that the stop plus fees loses the risk budget pays 0.08% ÷ (stop% + 0.08%) of it in fees, 0.04% on entry and 0.04% on exit: 0.08 ÷ 3.98 ≈ 2% for a 3.9% stop, 0.08 ÷ 0.38 ≈ 21% for a 0.3% stop, and 21% of $500 ≈ $105.
